While our results showcase the potential gains achievable through sampler improvements, they also highlight the main shortcoming of stochasticity: For best results, one must make several heuristic choices — either implicit or explicit — that depend on the speciﬁc model. Indeed, we had to ﬁnd the optimal values of {Schurn,Stmin,Stmax,Snoise}on a case-by-case basis using grid search (Appendix E.2). This raises a general concern that using stochastic sampling as the primary means of evaluating model improvements may inadvertently end up inﬂuencing the design choices related to model architecture and training. 5 Preconditioning and training There are various known good practices for training neural networks in a supervised fashion. For example, it is advisable to keep input and output signal magnitudes ﬁxed to, e.g., unit variance, and to avoid large variation in gradient magnitudes on a per-sample basis [5, 21]. Training a neural network to model Ddirectly would be far from ideal — for example, as the input x= y+ nis a combination of clean signal yand noise n∼N(0,σ2I), its magnitude varies immensely depending on noise level σ. For this reason, the common practice is to not represent Dθ as a neural network directly, but instead train a different network Fθ from which Dθ is derived. Previous methods [37, 47, 49] address the input scaling via a σ-dependent normalization factor and attempt to precondition the output by training Fθ to predict nscaled to unit variance, from which the signal is then reconstructed via Dθ(x; σ) = x−σFθ(·). This has the drawback that at large σ, the network needs to ﬁne-tune its output carefully to cancel out the existing noise nexactly and give the output at the correct scale; note that any errors made by the network are ampliﬁed by a factor of σ. In this situation, it would seem much easier to predict the expected output D(x; σ) directly. In the same spirit as previous parameterizations that adaptively mix signal and noise (e.g., [ 10, 44, 53]), we propose to precondition the neural network with a σ-dependent skip connection that allows it to estimate either yor n, or something in between. We thus write Dθ in the following form: Dθ(x; σ) = cskip(σ) x+ cout(σ) Fθ ( cin(σ) x; cnoise(σ) ) , (7) where Fθ is the neural network to be trained, cskip(σ) modulates the skip connection, cin(σ) and cout(σ) scale the input and output magnitudes, and cnoise(σ) maps noise level σinto a conditioning in- put for Fθ. The probabil- ity of sampling a given noise level σis given by ptrain(σ) and the corresponding weight is given by λ(σ). To prevent potential overﬁtting that often plagues diffusion models with smaller datasets, we borrow an augmentation pipeline from the GAN literature [25]. The pipeline consists of various geometric transformations (see Appendix F.2) that we apply to a training image prior to adding noise. To prevent the augmentations from leaking to the generated images, we provide the augmentation parameters as a conditioning input to Fθ; during inference we set the them to zero to guarantee that only non-augmented images are generated. Table 2 shows that data augmentation provides a consistent improvement (conﬁg F) that yields new state-of-the-art FIDs of 1.79 and 1.97 for conditional and unconditional CIFAR-10, beating the previous records of 1.85 [45] and 2.10 [53]. This suggests that more diverse datasets continue to beneﬁt from stochastic sampling. 6 Conclusions Our approach of putting diffusion models to a common framework exposes a modular design. This allows a targeted investigation of individual components, potentially helping to better cover the viable design space. In our tests this let us simply replace the samplers in various earlier models, drastically improving the results. For example, in ImageNet-64 our sampler turned an average model (FID 2.07) to a challenger (1.55) for the previous SOTA model (1.48) [ 17], and with training improvements achieved SOTA FID of 1.36. We also obtained new state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10 while using only 35 model evaluations, deterministic sampling, and a small network. The current high-resolution diffusion models rely either on separate super-resolution steps [17, 36, 40], subspace projection [23], very large networks [9, 49], or hybrid approaches [39, 42, 53] — we believe that our contributions are orthogonal to these extensions. That said, many of our parameter values may need to be re-adjusted for higher resolution datasets. Furthermore, we feel that the precise interaction between stochastic sampling and the training objective remains an interesting question for future work. Societal impact. Our advances in sample quality can potentially amplify negative societal effects when used in a large-scale system like DALL·E 2, including types of disinformation or emphasizing sterotypes and harmful biases [34]. B.5 Our SDE formulation (Eq. 6) We derive the SDE of Eq. 6 by the following strategy: • The desired marginal densities p ( x; σ(t) ) are convolutions of the data density pdata and an isotropic Gaussian density with standard deviation σ(t) (see Eq. 20). Hence, considered as a function of the time t, the density evolves according to a heat diffusion PDE with time-varying diffusivity. As a ﬁrst step, we ﬁnd this PDE. • We then use the Fokker–Planck equation to recover a family of SDEs for which the density evolves according to this PDE. Eq. 6 is obtained from a suitable parametrization of this family. B.5.1 Generating the marginals by heat diffusion We consider the time evolution of a probability density q(x,t). Our goal is to ﬁnd a PDE whose solution with the initial value q(x,0) := pdata(x) is q(x,t) = p ( x,σ(t) ) . That is, the PDE should reproduce the marginals we postulate in Eq. 20. The desired marginals are convolutions of pdata with isotropic normal distributions of time-varying standard deviation σ(t), and as such, can be generated by the heat equation with time-varying diffusivity κ(t). The situation is most conveniently analyzed in the Fourier domain, where the marginal densities are simply pointwise products of a Gaussian function and the transformed data density. To ﬁnd the diffusivity that induces the correct standard deviations, we ﬁrst write down the heat equation PDE: ∂q(x,t) ∂t = κ(t)∆xq(x,t). (82) The Fourier transformed counterpart of Eq. 82, where the transform is taken along the x-dimension, is given by ∂ˆq(ν,t) ∂t = −κ(t)|ν|2 ˆq(ν,t). [49]) on Eq. 103; the entire effect of the reversal is a change of sign in the middle term. The scaled generalization of the SDE can be derived using a similar approach as with the ODE previously. In practice, the original implementations of these methods differ considerably in terms of the deﬁnitions of model inputs and outputs, dynamic range of image data, scaling of x, and interpretation of σ. We eliminate this variation by standardizing on a uniﬁed setup where the model always matches our deﬁnition of Fθ, image data is always represented in the continuous range [−1,1], and the details of xand σare always in agreement with Eq. 4. We minimize the accumulation of ﬂoating point round-off errors by always executing Algorithms 1 and 2 at double precision (float64). However, we still execute the network Fθ(·) at single precision (float32) to minimize runtime and remain faithful to previous work in terms of network architecture. Speciﬁcally, given the value of xi−1 at time step i−1, the solver approximates the true x∗ i as xi, resulting in local truncation error τi = x∗ i −xi. The local errors get accumulated over the N steps, ultimately leading to global truncation error eN. Euler’s method is a ﬁrst order ODE solver, meaning thatτi = O ( h2 i ) for any sufﬁciently smooth x(t), where hi = |ti −ti−1|is the local step size [50]. In other words, there exist some C and H such that ||τi||< Ch2 i for every hi < H, i.e., halving hi reduces τi by 4×. Furthermore, if we assume that Dθ is Lipschitz continuous — which is true for all network architectures considered in this paper — the global truncation error is bounded by ||eN||≤ Emaxi||τi||, where the value of E depends on N, t0, tN, and the Lipschitz constant [ 50]. Thus, reducing the global error for given N, which in turn enables reducing N itself, boils down to choosing the solver and {ti}so that maxi||τi||is minimized. To gain insight on how the local truncation error behaves in practice, we measure the values of τi over different noise levels using the VE-based CIFAR-10 model. For a given noise level, we set ti = σ−1(σi) and choose some ti−1 > ti depending on the case. We then sample xi−1 from p(x; σi−1) and estimate the true x∗ i by performing 200 Euler steps over uniformly selected subintervals between ti−1 and t. Finally, we plot the mean and standard deviation of the root mean square error (RMSE), i.e., ||τi||/ √ dim τ, as a function of σi, averaged over 200 random samples of xi−1. Results for Euler’s method are shown in Figure 13a, where the blue curve corresponds to uniform step size hσ = 1.25 with respect to σ, i.e., σi−1 = σi + hσ and ti−1 = σ−1(σi−1). We see that the error is very large (RMSE ≈0.56) for low noise levels (σi ≤0.5) and considerably smaller for high noise levels. This is in line with the common intuition that, in order to reduce eN, the step size should be decreased monotonically with decreasing σ. Each curve is surrounded by a shaded region that indicates standard deviation, barely visible at low values ofσ. This indicates that τi is nearly constant with respect to xi−1, and thus there would be no beneﬁt in varying {ti}schedule on a per-sample basis. A convenient way to vary the local step size depending on the noise level is to deﬁne {σi}as a linear resampling of some monotonically increasing, unbounded warp function w(z). In other words, σi<N = w(Ai+ B) and σN = 0, where constants Aand B are selected so that σ0 = σmax and σN−1 = σmin. In practice, we set σmin = max(σlo,0.002) and σmax = min(σhi,80), where σlo and σhi are the lowest and highest noise levels supported by a given model, respectively; we have found these choices to perform reasonably well in practice. Now, to balance τi between low and high noise levels, we can, for example, use a polynomial warp function w(z) = zρ parameterized by the 39exponent ρ. This choice leads to the following formula for {σi}: σi<N = ( σmax 1 ρ + i N −1 ( σmin 1 ρ −σmax 1 ρ ))ρ ,σN = 0, (269) which reduces to uniform discretization when ρ= 1 and gives more and more emphasis to low noise levels as ρincreases.18 Based on the value of σi, we can now compute σi−1 = ( σ1/ρ i −A )ρ , which enables us to visualize τi for different choices of ρin Figure 13a. We see that increasing ρreduces the error for low noise levels (σ <10) while increasing it for high noise levels (σ >10). Approximate balance is achieved at ρ= 2, but RMSE remains relatively high (∼0.03), meaning that Euler’s method drifts away from the correct result by several ULPs at each step. While the error could be reduced by increasing N, we would ideally like the RMSE to be well below 0.01 even with low step counts. Heun’s method introduces an additional correction step forxi+1 to account for the fact that dx/dt may change between ti and ti+1; Euler’s method assumes it to be constant. The correction leads to cubic convergence of the local truncation error, i.e., τi = O ( h3 i ) , at the cost of one additional evaluation of Dθ per step. We discuss the general family of Heun-like schemes later in Appendix D.2. Figure 13b shows local truncation error for Heun’s method using the same setup as Figure 13a. We see that the differences in ||τi||are generally more pronounced, which is to be expected given the quadratic vs. cubic convergence of the two methods. Cases where Euler’s method has low RMSE tend to have even lower RMSE with Heun’s method, and vice versa for cases with high RMSE. Most remarkably, the red curve shows almost constant RMSE ∈[0.0030,0.0045]. This means that the combination of Eq. 269 and Heun’s method is, in fact, very close to optimal withρ= 3. Thus far, we have only considered the raw numerical error, i.e., component-wise deviation from the true result in RGB space. The raw numerical error is relevant for certain use cases, e.g., image manipulation where the ODE is ﬁrst evaluated in the direction of increasing tand then back to t= 0 again — in this case, ||eN||directly tells us how much the original image degrades in the process and we can use ρ = 3 to minimize it. Considering the generation of novel images from scratch, however, it is reasonable to expect different noise levels to introduce different kinds of errors that may not necessarily be on equal footing considering their perceptual importance. We investigate this in Figure 13c, where we plot FID as a function of ρfor different models and different choices of N. Note that the ImageNet-64 model was only trained for a discrete set of noise levels; in order to use it with Eq. 269, we round each ti to its nearest supported counterpart, i.e., t′ i = uarg minj|uj−ti|. From the plot, we can see that even though ρ = 3 leads to relatively good FID, it can be reduced further by choosing ρ> 3. This corresponds to intentionally introducing error at high noise levels to reduce it at low noise levels, which makes intuitive sense because the value ofσmax is somewhat arbitrary to begin with — increasing σmax can have a large impact on ||eN||, but it does not affect the resulting image distribution nearly as much. In general, we have found ρ= 7 to perform reasonably well in all cases, and use this value in all other experiments. D.2 General family of 2 nd order Runge–Kutta variants Heun’s method illustrated in Algorithm 1 belongs to a family of explicit two-stage 2nd order Runge– Kutta methods, each having the same computational cost. A common parameterization [50] of this family is, di = f(xi; ti) ; xi+1 = xi + h [( 1 − 1 2α ) di + 1 2αf(xi + αhdi; ti + αh) ] , (270) where h= ti+1 −ti and αis a parameter that controls where the additional gradient is evaluated and how much it inﬂuences the step taken. Setting α= 1 corresponds to Heun’s method, andα= 1 2 and α= 2 3 yield so-called midpoint and Ralston methods, respectively. All these variants differ in the kind of approximation error they incur due to the geometry of the underlying function f. E Further results with stochastic sampling E.1 Image degradation due to excessive stochastic iteration Figure 14 illustrates the image degradation caused by excessive Langevin iteration (Section 4, “Practical considerations”). These images are generated by doing a speciﬁed number of iterations at a ﬁxed noise level σso that at each iteration an equal amount of noise is added and removed. In theory, Langevin dynamics should bring the distribution towards the ideal distribution p(x; σ) but as noted in Section 4, this holds only if the denoiser Dθ(x; σ) induces a conservative vector ﬁeld in Eq. 3. As seen in the ﬁgure, it is clear that the image distribution suffers from repeated iteration in all cases, although the exact failure mode depends on dataset and noise level. For low noise levels (below 0.2 or so), the images tend to oversaturate starting at 2k iterations and become fully corrupted after that. Our heuristic of setting Stmin >0 is designed to prevent stochastic sampling altogether at very low noise levels to avoid this effect. For high noise levels, we can see that iterating without the standard deviation correction, i.e., when Snoise = 1.000, the images tend to become more abstract and devoid of color at high iteration counts; this is especially visible in the 10k column of CIFAR-10 where the images become mostly black and white with no discernible backgrounds. Our heuristic inﬂation of standard deviation by setting Snoise >1 counteracts this tendency efﬁciently, as seen in the corresponding images on the right hand side of the ﬁgure. To reduce the impact of random variation, typically in the order of ±2%, we compute FID three times in each experiment and report the minimum. F.2 Augmentation regularization In Section 5, we propose to combat overﬁtting of Dθ using conditional augmentation. We build our augmentation pipeline around the same concepts that were originally proposed by Karras et al. [25] in the context of GANs. In practice, we employ a set of 6 geometric transformations; we have found other types of augmentations, such as color corruption and image-space ﬁltering, to be consistently harmful for diffusion-based models. The details of our augmentation pipeline are shown in Table 6. We apply the augmentations indepen- dently to each training image y∼pdata prior to adding the noise n∼N(0,σ2I). First, we determine whether to enable or disable each augmentation based on a weighted coin toss. The probability of enabling a given augmentation (“Prob.” column) is ﬁxed to 12% for CIFAR-10 and 15% for FFHQ and AFHQv2, except for x-ﬂips that are always enabled. We then draw 8 random parameters from their corresponding distributions (“Parameters” column); if a given augmentation is disabled, we override the associated parameters with zero. Based on these, we construct a homogeneous 2D transformation matrix based on the parameters (“Transformation” column). This transformation is applied to the image using the implementation of [25] that employs 2×supersampled high-quality Wavelet ﬁlters. Finally, we construct a 9-dimensional conditioning input vector (“Conditioning” column) and feed it to the denoiser network, in addition to the image and noise level inputs. The role of the conditioning input is to present the network with a set of auxiliary tasks; in addition to the main task of modeling p(x; σ), we effectively ask the network to also model an inﬁnite set of distributions p(x; σ,a) for each possible choice of the augmentation parameters a. With our non-leaky augmentations, we get the same beneﬁts without the downsides by executing the x-ﬂip augmentation with 100% probability. Thus, we rely exclusively on our augmentation scheme and disable dataset x-ﬂips to ensure that the generated images stay true to the original distribution. We trained each model until a total of 200 million images had been drawn from the training set, abbreviated as “200 Mimg” in Table 7; this corresponds to a total of∼400,000 training iterations using a batch size of 512. We saved a snapshot of the model every 2.5 million images and reported results for the snapshot that achieved the lowest FID according to our deterministic sampler with NFE= 35 or NFE = 79, depending on the resolution. In conﬁg B, we re-adjust the basic hyperparameters to enable faster training and obtain a more meaningful point of comparison. Speciﬁcally, we increase the parallelism from 4 to 8 GPUs and batch size from 128 to 512 or 256, depending on the resolution. We also disable gradient clipping, i.e., forcing ∥dL(Dθ)/dθ∥2 ≤1, that we found to provide no beneﬁt in practice. In practice, we store the trainable parameters as FP32 but cast them to FP16 when evaluating Fθ, except for the embedding and self-attention layers, where we found the limited exponent range of FP16 to occasionally lead to stability issues. We trained the model for two weeks, corresponding to ∼2500 million images drawn from the training set and ∼600,000 training iterations, using learning rate 0.0001, exponential moving average of 50 million images, and the same model architecture and dropout probability as Dhariwal and Nichol [9]. We did not ﬁnd overﬁtting to be a concern, and thus chose to not employ augmentation regularization. F.4 Network architectures As a result of our training improvements, the VP and VE cases become otherwise identical in con- ﬁg F except for the network architecture; VP employs the DDPM++ architecture while VE employs NCSN++, both of which were originally proposed by Song et al. [ 49]. These architectures corre- spond to relatively straightforward variations of the same U-net backbone with three differences, as illustrated in Table 8. First, DDPM++ employs box ﬁlter [1,1] for the upsampling and downsampling layers whereas NCSN++ employs bilinear ﬁlter [1,3,3,1]. Second, DDPM++ inherits its positional encoding scheme for the noise level directly from DDPM [ 16] whereas NCSN++ replaces it with random Fourier features [ 52]. Third, NCSN ++ incorporates additional residual skip connections from the input image to each block in the encoder, as explained in Appendix H of [49] (“progressive growing architectures”). For class conditioning and augmentation regularization, we extend the original DDPM ++ and NCSN++ arhictectures by introducing two optional conditioning inputs alongside the noise level input. We represent class labels as one-hot encoded vectors that we ﬁrst scale by √ C, where C is the total number of classes, and then feed through a fully-connected layer. For the augmentation parameters, we feed the conditioning inputs of Appendix F.2 through a fully-connected layer as-is. 46We then combine the resulting feature vectors with the original noise level conditioning vector through elementwise addition. For class-conditional ImageNet-64, we use the ADM architecture of Dhariwal and Nichol [9] with no changes. The model has a total of ∼296 million trainable parameters. As detailed in Tables 7 and 8, the most notable differences to DDPM ++ include the use of a slightly shallower model (3 residual blocks per resolution instead of 4) with considerably more channels (e.g., 768 in the lowest resolution instead of 256), more self-attention layers interspersed throughout the network (22 instead of 6), and the use of multi-head attention (e.g., 12 heads in the lowest resolution). We feel that the precise impact of architectural choices remains an interesting question for future work. new_method.method:
Open Problems: Current memory–saving techniques for diffusion models are almost exclusively post-hoc (caching, pruning, quantisation) and focus on inference.  During full-model pre-training or large-scale finetuning the standard U-Net/Transformer backbones still require storing hundreds of MB of activations and parameters, making high-resolution or long-video training infeasible on commodity GPUs.  A principled architecture that is intrinsically memory–efficient both in forward *and* backward passes – without a quality penalty – is still missing.
Methods: We propose RevMoDiff (Reversible & Modular Diffusion Network).  Key ideas:
1. Reversible Dual-Stream Blocks: Replace every ResNet/Transformer block in the noise-predictor with an invertible pair of affine coupling layers.  During back-prop we recompute activations instead of storing them, giving O(1) activation memory.
2. Parameter Condensation: All blocks share a single parameter bank W; a lightweight FiLM-like ‘weight composer’ M(t, l, c) generates block-specific weights on-the-fly as low-rank modulations of W using time-step t, layer index l and (optional) text condition c.  Only the shared bank is kept in GPU memory; the tiny composer runs in FP16.
3. Progressive Refinement Columns: The network is organised into K columns of increasing receptive field.  At early/noisy timesteps only column 0 is executed; later columns are enabled adaptively (learned gate).  This yields depth-adaptive computation similar to caching but *architecturally* built-in, so no stored features are required.
4. Intrinsic Feature Slicing: Inside every reversible block we process channels in G groups sequentially (feature micro-batching) so that peak feature maps never exceed 1 ⁄ G of the usual size; groups are fused by a shuffle operation.
5. Training recipe: We train from scratch with standard DDPM or v-prediction loss.  Because blocks are reversible we checkpoint nothing; because weights are shared the parameter count shrinks ≈4×.  We add a distillation regulariser to a full U-Net teacher to keep sample quality.
6. Inference: Progressive gates + group slicing give the same memory footprint as Streamlined Inference but require no graph surgery.  Columns/gates can be frozen or optimised by L2C-style routers.
Novelty vs prior work: Unlike Hollowed Net (temporary pruning) or DeepCache (store & reuse), RevMoDiff avoids storing activations altogether; unlike DiT/SSM works it focuses on *memory* not FLOPs; unlike reversible GAN works we integrate adaptive depth and shared weights for diffusion.
Experimental Setup: Datasets & tasks
• ImageNet-1K 256² and 512² class-conditional generation.
• MS-COCO 2014 text-to-image (Stable-Diffusion latent space, keep SD VAE).
• UCF-101 16-frame 512² video with latent-diffusion baseline (to test spatio-temporal variant).
Baselines
• Standard UNet (ADM) and DiT backbones with 1-GPU activation checkpointing.
• Hollowed Net fine-tuning (memory only in FT stage).
• DeepCache, L2C, Streamlined Inference (for inference memory/latency).
Metrics
Training: peak GPU memory, images/sec, FID / IS / CLIP on validation.
Inference: peak memory, latency per image/video, FVD (video).
Ablations
(1) effect of number of reversible columns K; (2) group size G; (3) without teacher distillation; (4) adaptive gates vs fixed depth.
Robustness
• 1024² unconditional generation on single 24 GB GPU (show feasibility).
• Personalisation: DreamBooth LoRA on 8 GB GPU using RevMoDiff backbone.
Implementation details
• PyTorch + custom reversible blocks (no extra CUDA); composer is 2-layer MLP; training on 8×A100 for 400k steps.
Result: We expect:
• Peak *training* memory reduced by ≈60 % versus ADM (e.g. 18 GB → 7 GB for 512²), enabling 1024² on 24 GB.
• Parameter count ↓4×, FLOPs unchanged for full depth; with adaptive gates average FLOPs ↓45 %.
• FID/ImageNet-256: 3.1 (ADM: 3.0).  COCO CLIP score unchanged (0.32 vs 0.32).  Video FVD within 2 % of baseline.
• Inference latency similar to DeepCache (1.6× speed-up) but with <50 % peak memory of DeepCache because no caches stored.
• Personalisation quality parity with Hollowed Net while using <6 GB memory.
Conclusion: RevMoDiff shows that memory bottlenecks in diffusion models can be solved *architecturally* rather than by post-hoc tricks.  A single 24 GB card can now train or finetune 1024² diffusion models, broadening access to high-fidelity generation and facilitating research on even larger contexts (long videos, 3D).  The reversible-shared-weight design is orthogonal to quantisation or pruning and can be combined for further gains.  Future work: extend composer to dynamic SSM backbones, investigate hardware-aware column scheduling, and explore theoretical links between reversibility and diffusion stochastic inverses.

experimental_design.experiment_strategy:
Below are three concrete, Python-feasible experimental plans to validate RevMoDiff from complementary angles: training-time memory/quality, adaptive depth for compute savings (with inference memory/latency), and high-resolution feasibility.

========================================================================
Experiment 1 — Training-time memory and quality parity on ImageNet-256/512
========================================================================
Goal
- Demonstrate that RevMoDiff reduces peak training memory by ≈60% and parameters by ≈4× versus standard ADM/DiT while matching sample quality (FID/IS/CLIP) and maintaining comparable throughput.

Dataset
- ImageNet-1K, class-conditional. Two settings: 256×256 and 512×512.

Models
- Baselines: ADM-UNet (class-conditional), DiT-S/XL (class-conditional), both with activation checkpointing.
- Ours: RevMoDiff with reversible dual-stream blocks, weight composer, columns (K), and group slicing (G). For fairness in the core memory/quality comparison, keep all columns enabled during training (adaptive gates off), then run ablations.

Metrics
- Training: peak GPU memory (MiB), images/sec, parameter count, average activation memory (tracked via torch.cuda), and per-step wall-clock.
- Validation: FID (ImageNet subset protocol with 50k samples), IS, CLIP score (for class-conditional labels via prompt templates), NFE at inference.

Protocol
1) Teacher model for distillation: use a strong ADM teacher (public weights or trained baseline). Freeze teacher.
2) Training loss: v-pred or epsilon loss + distillation regularizer L_distill = λ * MSE(h_student, h_teacher) at selected intermediate layers or final noise prediction.
3) Train 400k steps on 8×A100 (40GB), mixed precision (fp16/bf16), AdamW.
4) Memory tracking: torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats(); log torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() every 100 steps; cross-check with nvidia-smi.
5) Evaluation: generate 50k samples; compute FID/IS; evaluate CLIP retrieval score.
6) Report: memory, throughput, parameters, and quality metrics vs ADM and DiT.

Ablations (run on 256×256 to contain cost)
- K: 1, 2, 3 columns (gates off; always full depth).
- G (group slicing): 1, 2, 4, 8.
- Distillation: on vs off.
- Weight sharing: composer vs no-sharing (distinct per-block weights) with matched FLOPs.
- Reversibility: reversible vs standard residual blocks with activation checkpointing.

Acceptance criteria
- Peak training memory reduced by ≈60% at 512×512 versus ADM+ckpt.
- Parameter count ≈4× smaller with no worse than +5% FID degradation (e.g., ≤3.15 if ADM=3.0 at 256×256).
- Throughput equal or within 10% of baseline with full depth.

Time/Compute budget
- Full run: 8×A100, 400k steps, global batch 256 for 256²; scale down for 512² if needed; measure at matched batch sizes for a fair memory comparison.

Minimal code scaffold (key parts)

class RevAffineCoupling(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, ch, cond_ch):
        super().__init__()
        # s,t nets can be light convs/attn blocks using composed weights
        self.s_net = nn.Sequential(nn.GroupNorm(32, ch//2), nn.SiLU(), nn.Conv2d(ch//2, ch//2, 3, padding=1), nn.Conv2d(ch//2, ch//2, 1))
        self.t_net = nn.Sequential(nn.GroupNorm(32, ch//2), nn.SiLU(), nn.Conv2d(ch//2, ch//2, 3, padding=1), nn.Conv2d(ch//2, ch//2, 1))
    def forward(self, x):
        x1, x2 = torch.chunk(x, 2, dim=1)
        s = torch.tanh(self.s_net(x1))
        t = self.t_net(x1)
        y2 = x2 * torch.exp(s) + t
        y = torch.cat([x1, y2], dim=1)
        return y
    def inverse(self, y):
        y1, y2 = torch.chunk(y, 2, dim=1)
        s = torch.tanh(self.s_net(y1))
        t = self.t_net(y1)
        x2 = (y2 - t) * torch.exp(-s)
        x = torch.cat([y1, x2], dim=1)
        return x

class ReversibleBlock(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x, module):
        with torch.no_grad():
            y = module.forward(x)
        ctx.module = module
        ctx.save_for_backward(y)  # tiny foot-print; store only output
        return y
    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, dy):
        (y,) = ctx.saved_tensors
        with torch.no_grad():
            x = ctx.module.inverse(y)
        x.requires_grad_(True)
        with torch.enable_grad():
            y_re = ctx.module.forward(x)
        torch.autograd.backward(y_re, dy)
        dx = x.grad
        return dx, None

class WeightComposer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, W_shapes, rank=8, cond_dim=256):
        super().__init__()
        self.W_bank = nn.ParameterList([nn.Parameter(torch.randn(*s) * 0.02) for s in W_shapes])
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(cond_dim, 256), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(256, sum([(s[0]*s[1]) for s in W_shapes]) * 2))
        self.rank = rank
    def forward(self, cond):
        # cond includes t, layer index l, class/text embedding c
        v = self.mlp(cond)
        # For brevity, pretend v maps to low-rank updates for each W
        composed = []
        offset = 0
        for W in self.W_bank:
            flat = W.view(W.size(0), -1)
            # toy: scale-and-shift modulation; replace with low-rank UDV^T if needed
            scale = torch.tanh(v[..., offset:offset+flat.numel()].view_as(flat))
            offset += flat.numel()
            bias = v[..., offset:offset+flat.numel()].view_as(flat)
            offset += flat.numel()
            W_mod = (flat * (1 + 0.1*scale) + 0.1*bias).view_as(W)
            composed.append(W_mod)
        return composed

# Group slicing utility

def group_slice_forward(module, x, G):
    C = x.shape[1]
    assert C % G == 0
    gsz = C // G
    outs = []
    for g in range(G):
        xs = x[:, g*gsz:(g+1)*gsz]
        outs.append(module(xs))
    y = torch.cat(outs, dim=1)
    # optional channel shuffle here
    return y

# Memory instrumentation

def log_gpu_memory(tag):
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    mem = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / (1024**2)
    print(f"{tag} peak_mem(MiB)={mem:.1f}")

# Training step sketch

def train_step(model, teacher, batch, optimizer, scaler, lambda_distill):
    x0, y = batch  # image, label
    t = torch.randint(0, model.num_timesteps, (x0.size(0),), device=x0.device)
    noise = torch.randn_like(x0)
    xt = model.q_sample(x0, t, noise)
    with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():
        eps_hat = model(xt, t, y)  # RevMoDiff
        loss_main = F.mse_loss(eps_hat, noise)
        with torch.no_grad():
            eps_teacher = teacher(xt, t, y)
        loss_distill = F.mse_loss(eps_hat, eps_teacher)
        loss = loss_main + lambda_distill * loss_distill
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    scaler.step(optimizer)
    scaler.update()

How to run
- Implement RevMoDiff with the above building blocks, start with K=2 columns, G=4 groups for 512².
- Baselines: use public ADM/DiT implementations with torch.utils.checkpoint on every residual block.
- Log peak memory and throughput regularly; run evaluation jobs to compute FID/IS/CLIP.

Expected results
- ~60% training memory reduction at 512² (e.g., 18 GB → ≈7 GB) vs ADM+ckpt, 4× fewer parameters, FID within 0.1–0.2 absolute at 256²; CLIP parity.


=============================================================================================
Experiment 2 — Adaptive columns for compute savings and inference mem/latency vs DeepCache
=============================================================================================
Goal
- Show that RevMoDiff’s progressive refinement columns (with learned gates) reduce average FLOPs ≈45% while preserving quality, and achieve inference latency comparable to DeepCache/Streamlined Inference but with lower peak memory due to no feature caches.

Dataset
- MS-COCO 2014 (Karpathy split), text-to-image in Stable Diffusion latent space (keep SD VAE). Use captions as conditions.

Models
- Baseline A: SD-UNet (latent), standard inference.
- Baseline B: SD-UNet + DeepCache (or Streamlined Inference) during inference only.
- Ours: RevMoDiff-latent with K columns and group slicing G; weight composer uses text embeddings; learned gate g_k(t, c) per column.

Metrics
- Training: peak memory, images/sec.
- Inference: latency per 50 sampling steps, peak memory (MiB), FLOPs (fvcore or torch.profiler), average active columns per timestep, CLIP score (image-text), FID@30k.

Protocol
1) Convert to latent-diffusion: freeze SD VAE; train RevMoDiff-latent on COCO for 300k steps.
2) Gate training: initialize fixed schedule (early timesteps use column 0 only), then train gates g_k(t,c) via distillation to SD teacher with a small penalty α * sum_k g_k to encourage sparsity. Optionally train with L2C-style supervised labels indicating minimal columns needed to match teacher’s intermediate features.
3) Inference settings: same NFE across models (e.g., 50 DDIM steps). For DeepCache baseline, set recommended cache interval.
4) Measure: latency and peak memory for batch=4 on a single A100; also test batch=1 on a 24GB consumer GPU if possible.
5) Quality: compute CLIP score and FID on 30k COCO validation samples.

Ablations
- Gates: learned vs fixed schedule vs always-full-depth.
- K: 2 vs 3 columns; G: 1, 2, 4.
- Composer precision: FP16 vs BF16.

Acceptance criteria
- Average columns active < 2.0 with K=3; ≈45% FLOP reduction.
- Inference latency 1.4–1.7× faster vs baseline SD-UNet; within ±0.02 CLIP score and ≤5% FID delta.
- Peak inference memory < 50% of DeepCache at same speed (no caches stored).

Minimal code scaffold (gates + profiling)

class ColumnGater(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_cols, cond_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(cond_dim+1, 128), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(128, num_cols))
    def forward(self, t_norm, text_emb):
        # t_norm in [0,1]; text_emb from CLIP/T5
        h = torch.cat([t_norm[:,None], text_emb], dim=1)
        logits = self.mlp(h)
        gates = torch.sigmoid(logits)  # soft gates in training, hard threshold in eval
        return gates

def run_inference(model, cond, steps=50):
    torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
    start = time.time()
    imgs = model.sample(cond, steps=steps)  # inside, apply gates per step
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    latency = time.time() - start
    peak = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / (1024**2)
    return imgs, latency, peak

# FLOPs estimation (rough)
from fvcore.nn import FlopCountAnalysis
flops = FlopCountAnalysis(model, (dummy_xt, dummy_t, dummy_cond)).total()

Expected results
- With K=3, learned gates skip late columns for early/noisy timesteps, cutting ~45% FLOPs, matching CLIP and near-identical FID. Peak memory notably smaller than DeepCache since no feature buffers are stored.


=====================================================================================
Experiment 3 — 1024×1024 training feasibility on a single 24 GB GPU (stress test)
=====================================================================================
Goal
- Validate RevMoDiff enables practical 1024² training on commodity 24 GB GPUs, impossible with standard ADM without extreme checkpointing or tiny batch sizes. Optionally, show low-memory personalization via LoRA on 8 GB GPU.

Dataset
- ImageNet-1K resized to 1024×1024 (unconditional or class-conditional). For a quick feasibility demo, unconditional training suffices; class-conditioning increases memory slightly due to embeddings.

Models
- Baseline: ADM-UNet with activation checkpointing; attempt to run with batch=1 at 1024².
- Ours: RevMoDiff with K=2 columns, G=8 group slicing, composer in FP16.

Metrics
- Training: successful forward+backward at 1024², peak memory, images/sec, stability (loss curve), samples for visual inspection.
- Optional quality: preliminary FID on 10k samples after 50k steps (focus here is feasibility, not SOTA quality).

Protocol
1) Single-GPU setup: 24 GB (e.g., RTX 3090/4090). Use gradient accumulation to reach effective batch size 8–16; AMP on.
2) Ours: enable reversibility (no activation checkpoints), G=8, K=2 (gates off for fairness), mixed precision, composer in FP16.
3) Baseline ADM: try to run with same optimizer and grad accumulation; record OOM conditions and minimal workable configuration, if any.
4) Log peak memory per step; ensure nvidia-smi verify. Save wall-clock per step for both models.
5) After 50k steps, sample 2k images to verify reasonable training behavior.

Optional extension: Personalization on 8 GB
- DreamBooth LoRA fine-tune RevMoDiff at 512² on a single 8 GB GPU: batch=1, grad accumulation, LoRA rank=8 on composer and final convs; compare to Hollowed Net in memory and output quality.

Acceptance criteria
- RevMoDiff runs 1024² training with peak memory ≤24 GB, batch≥1, stable losses. ADM either OOMs or requires much smaller effective batch / extreme checkpointing with significantly worse throughput.

Minimal code scaffold (feasibility harness)

def can_train_1024(model):

        torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()

# LoRA quick attach (composer and final convs)

Expected results
- Demonstrates practical 1024² training on 24 GB with RevMoDiff, while baseline struggles. Optional LoRA shows ≤6 GB memory during personalization with comparable visual quality.


General implementation notes (applies to all experiments)
- Use PyTorch 2.x, torch.compile where stable; mixed precision (bf16 on A100, fp16 on consumer GPUs).
- Use deterministic dataloader seeds for fair comparisons; 3 seeds per experiment where feasible.
- For FID/IS/CLIP, use reliable implementations (torch-fidelity, clean-fid, open-clip) and report 95% CIs when running multiple seeds.
- Ensure same sampler, same NFE, and same VAE for latent experiments when comparing inference.
- Log everything with WandB or TensorBoard: memory, throughput, loss, gate activations, column usage, FLOPs, and metrics.

Summary of expected takeaways
- Experiment 1: Architectural memory savings during training (not just inference) without quality drop; parameter condensation works.
- Experiment 2: Built-in adaptive depth cuts compute and inference memory without caching, matching DeepCache-like speed.
- Experiment 3: High-res 1024² training on a 24 GB GPU becomes feasible; optional 8 GB personalization confirms low-memory fine-tuning.
experimental_design.experiment_details:
Below I elaborate each item in the Experiment Strategy and extend it with concrete, PyTorch-feasible implementation details, reliability measures, and non-overlapping ablations. I rely on existing Python libraries where possible: MemCNN (reversible wrapping), FrEIA (alternative invertible framework), diffusers (latent diffusion), peft (LoRA), clean-fid and torch-fidelity (metrics), open-clip (CLIP), fvcore (FLOPs), accelerate (DDP + mixed precision), xformers (memory-efficient attention), and wandb/TensorBoard for logging. I avoid custom CUDA.

============================================================
Experiment 1 — Training-time memory and quality parity (ImageNet-256/512)
============================================================
Goal
- Show that RevMoDiff cuts peak training memory by ~60% and parameters by ~4× vs ADM/DiT while keeping FID/IS/CLIP parity and similar throughput.
- Keep adaptive gates off to isolate architectural memory savings from reversible blocks, weight composer, and group slicing.

Dataset
- ImageNet-1K with class labels.
- Two runs: 256×256 and 512×512.
- Dataloading: torchvision.datasets.ImageNet or WebDataset shards; transforms: random resized crop, flip, normalize.

Baselines
- ADM-UNet (class-conditional), official guided-diffusion implementation or lucidrains/ADM equivalent; enable torch.utils.checkpoint on each residual or attention block.
- DiT-S/XL (class-conditional), official repo, enable checkpointing on transformer blocks.

Ours (RevMoDiff; gates OFF)
- Backbone: reversible dual-stream affine coupling blocks wrapped via MemCNN’s InvertibleModuleWrapper for O(1) activation memory.
- Parameter condensation: one shared parameter bank W across blocks; a FiLM/LoRA-like composer M(t, l, c) produces low-rank modulations of conv/linear weights on the fly. Composer runs fp16/bf16.
- Intrinsic feature slicing: process channels in G groups sequentially inside each reversible block to cap peak activations to 1/G.
- Progressive columns: K columns stacked from small to large receptive field; for this experiment, keep all columns active to avoid confounding compute savings.
- Distillation: epsilon/v-pred MSE vs a frozen ADM teacher. Optionally add intermediate feature distillation via a single 1×1 projection to keep memory modest.

Reproducibility and reliability controls
- 3 seeds (e.g., 0, 1, 2). Seed torch, numpy, random; set cudnn.benchmark=False, cudnn.deterministic=True when measuring exact reproducibility. For main runs, allow benchmark=True for throughput.
- Log peak memory using torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated and cross-check with nvidia-smi.
- Use ExponentialMovingAverage (EMA) of weights for evaluation.
- Gradient clipping (value 1.0) to stabilize training at 512².
- Sanity checks: reversible round-trip error and gradient parity tests (see below).

Key hyperparameters
- Optimizer: AdamW(lr=1e-4 at 256², 7.5e-5 at 512², betas=(0.9,0.99), wd=0.01), cosine LR schedule with warmup 10k steps.
- Loss: v-prediction preferred; distillation coefficient λ=0.2 initially; tune in [0.05, 0.3].
- K columns: default 2 for 512²; 1 for 256² in ablation. G: default 4 for 512²; 2 for 256².
- Training: 400k steps, batch size per GPU such that baseline fits with checkpointing; AMP (bf16 on A100, fp16 on consumer GPUs). 8×A100.

Metrics and measurement
- Training: peak GPU memory, images/sec, params (sum(p.numel()) for p.requires_grad), max activation tensor size, step wall-clock.
- Validation: FID/IS (clean-fid or torch-fidelity), CLIP score using open-clip ViT-H/14; 50k samples for FID at 256²; 30k acceptable for interim.
- NFE: fixed sampler (DDIM 50) across models.

Non-overlapping ablations (run at 256² to contain cost)
- K in {1, 2, 3} (gates off).
- G in {1, 2, 4, 8}.
- Distillation on/off.
- Weight sharing: composer vs no sharing (per-block weights) at same FLOPs.
- Reversibility: reversible vs vanilla residual + checkpointing.

Acceptance criteria
- ≈60% memory reduction at 512² vs ADM+checkpoint at matched microbatch.
- ~4× parameter reduction with ≤5% relative degradation in FID; throughput within 10%.

Implementation snippets

1) Reversible affine coupling with MemCNN

from memcnn import InvertibleModuleWrapper
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class STNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, ch_in, ch_hidden):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.GroupNorm(32, ch_in), nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(ch_in, ch_hidden, 3, padding=1), nn.SiLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(ch_hidden, ch_in * 2, 3, padding=1)  # outputs [s, t]
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        st = self.net(x)
        s, t = st.chunk(2, dim=1)
        s = torch.tanh(s)
        return s, t

class AffineCoupling(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, ch, hidden):
        super().__init__()
        self.st = STNet(ch // 2, hidden)
    def forward(self, x):  # x = [x1, x2]
        x1, x2 = x.chunk(2, dim=1)
        s, t = self.st(x1)
        y2 = x2 * torch.exp(s) + t
        return torch.cat([x1, y2], dim=1)
    def inverse(self, y):
        y1, y2 = y.chunk(2, dim=1)
        s, t = self.st(y1)
        x2 = (y2 - t) * torch.exp(-s)
        return torch.cat([y1, x2], dim=1)

# Wrap with MemCNN to reconstruct inputs during backward (O(1) activations)
rev_block = InvertibleModuleWrapper(fn=AffineCoupling(ch=256, hidden=512), keep_input=False, keep_input_inverse=False)

Note: MemCNN takes care of backward recomputation; no custom autograd needed.

2) Weight Composer (LoRA-like low-rank modulations on a shared bank)

import einops

class WeightComposer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, W_shapes, cond_dim=256, rank=8):
        super().__init__()
        self.W_bank = nn.ParameterList([nn.Parameter(torch.randn(*s) * 0.02) for s in W_shapes])
        self.rank = rank
        self.cond_to_AB = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(cond_dim, 256), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(256, sum([ (s[0]*rank + rank*s[1]) for s in W_shapes ])))
        self.register_buffer('scale', torch.tensor(0.1))
    def forward(self, cond):
        # cond: [B, cond_dim]; here we assume per-batch composition (broadcast to batch)
        v = self.cond_to_AB(cond)  # [B, sum]
        composed = []
        offset = 0
        for W in self.W_bank:
            out_ch, in_ch, *k = W.shape
            flatA = out_ch * self.rank
            flatB = self.rank * in_ch
            A = v[:, offset:offset+flatA].view(-1, out_ch, self.rank)  # [B, O, r]
            offset += flatA
            B = v[:, offset:offset+flatB].view(-1, self.rank, in_ch)   # [B, r, I]
            offset += flatB
            # low-rank delta
            delta = torch.matmul(A, B)  # [B, O, I]
            if len(k) == 2:  # conv2d kernel
                delta = delta[..., None, None].expand(-1, -1, -1, k[0], k[1])
                Wb = W.unsqueeze(0).expand(delta.size(0), -1, -1, -1, -1)
            elif len(k) == 0:  # linear
                Wb = W.unsqueeze(0)
            else:
                raise NotImplementedError
            W_mod = Wb + self.scale * delta
            composed.append(W_mod)
        return composed  # list of [B, ...]-shaped weights

# Stateless call helper (PyTorch 2.0) for modules using composed weights
from torch.nn.utils._stateless import functional_call

def apply_composed_weights(module, composed_weights, x):
    # map parameter names in module to tensors from composer; keep others as-is
    params = {name: p for name, p in module.named_parameters()}
    buffers = dict(module.named_buffers())
    # Replace selected keys
    for (name, _), W_mod in zip(module.named_parameters(), composed_weights):
        params[name] = W_mod.mean(dim=0)  # broadcast across batch for simplicity
    return functional_call(module, (params, buffers), (x,))

In practice, for speed and simplicity, we modulate per-layer norms with FiLM (scale/shift) and only LoRA-modulate a subset of heavy convs/linears.

3) Group slicing wrapper (process channels sequentially to limit peak activation size)

def group_slice(module, x, groups=4):
    C = x.shape[1]
    assert C % groups == 0
    gsz = C // groups
    outs = []
    for g in range(groups):
        xs = x[:, g*gsz:(g+1)*gsz]
        ys = module(xs)
        outs.append(ys)
    y = torch.cat(outs, dim=1)
    return y  # optional channel shuffle here

4) Teacher distillation training step (AMP + memory logging)

import time
from torch.cuda.amp import GradScaler, autocast

scaler = GradScaler()

def log_peak(tag):
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print(f"{tag} peak(MiB)={torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()/1024**2:.1f}")

def train_step(student, teacher, batch, optimizer, lambda_distill=0.2):
    x0, y = batch  # images, class labels
    t = torch.randint(0, student.num_timesteps, (x0.size(0),), device=x0.device)
    noise = torch.randn_like(x0)
    xt = student.q_sample(x0, t, noise)
    with autocast():
        eps_s = student(xt, t, y)
        loss_main = F.mse_loss(eps_s, noise)
        with torch.no_grad():
            eps_t = teacher(xt, t, y)
        loss_dist = F.mse_loss(eps_s, eps_t)
        loss = loss_main + lambda_distill * loss_dist
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    scaler.step(optimizer)
    scaler.update()
    return loss.item()

5) FID/IS/CLIP evaluation helpers

# clean-fid (pip install clean-fid)
from cleanfid import fid

def compute_fid(gen_dir, ref_name='imagenet_val_256'):  # precomputed stats name
    return fid.compute_fid(gen_dir, dataset_name=ref_name)

# torch-fidelity (pip install torch-fidelity)
from torch_fidelity import calculate_metrics
metrics = calculate_metrics(input1=gen_dir, input2='cifar10-train', metrics=['fid', 'is'])

# open-clip (pip install open-clip-torch)
import open_clip

model, _, preprocess = open_clip.create_model_and_transforms('ViT-H-14', pretrained='laion2b_s32b_b79k')
clip_tokenizer = open_clip.get_tokenizer('ViT-H-14')

def clip_score(images, texts):
    with torch.no_grad():
        txt = clip_tokenizer(texts).cuda()
        txt_emb = model.encode_text(txt)
        img_emb = model.encode_image(preprocess(images).cuda())
        img_emb = img_emb / img_emb.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        txt_emb = txt_emb / txt_emb.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        sims = (img_emb * txt_emb).sum(dim=-1)
    return sims.mean().item()

Validation and sanity procedures
- Reversibility check: for a random x, assert ||inverse(forward(x)) − x|| / ||x|| < 1e-5 across representative batches.
- Gradient parity: disable MemCNN, run a small model with checkpointing; compare gradients numerically (cosine similarity > 0.999 for key weights).
- Memory accounting: wrap step with torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats() and log peaks; ensure no leak by monitoring after torch.cuda.empty_cache() across epochs.

Expected outcome
- Training memory at 512² reduced from ~18 GB to ~7 GB at matched microbatch; parameters ~4× fewer; FID on ImageNet-256 within 0.1–0.2 absolute vs ADM; throughput within ±10%.


====================================================================
Experiment 2 — Adaptive columns for compute savings and inference mem/latency
====================================================================
Goal
- Validate that progressive refinement columns with learned gates reduce average FLOPs by ~45% and reach similar or better inference latency to DeepCache/Streamlined Inference with lower peak memory (no feature caches), while maintaining quality on MS-COCO latent diffusion.

Dataset and setup
- MS-COCO 2014 (Karpathy split). Text-to-image.
- Use latent diffusion: freeze SD VAE from diffusers (stabilityai/stable-diffusion-2-1-base VAE) and operate in latent space.
- Text encoder: CLIP text encoder as in SD, or T5 if following SDXL; to minimize drift, stick to SD v1.x text encoder via diffusers.

Baselines
- Baseline A: SD-UNet (latent) standard inference, 50 DDIM steps.
- Baseline B: SD-UNet + DeepCache or Streamlined Inference. Use publicly available DeepCache repo/settings; for Streamlined Inference, use diffusers built-in attention/CPU-ofload improvements to emulate speed-ups if DeepCache integration is unavailable.

Ours (RevMoDiff-latent)
- Same latent dimensionality and VAE as baseline for apples-to-apples.
- K=3 columns; G default 2 to balance speed/memory in latent space.
- Column gating: learn g_k(t, c) in [0, 1] via an MLP over normalized timestep and text embedding; straight-through hard threshold at eval.
- Sparsity penalty: α * sum_k g_k; anneal α from 0 to 1e-3 over first 50k steps to avoid under-training deep columns.
- Distillation: MSE between our eps/v-pred and SD teacher; feature distillation at selected U-Net mid-block for stability.

Training protocol
- Train 300k steps, batch size 256 global (adjust as needed); A100 bf16.
- Initially use fixed schedule to warm-start: only column 0 for first 25% of timesteps, columns 0–1 for next 50%, all columns for final 25%; then unfreeze gates and optimize.
- Gating implementation: hard-concrete L0 (Louizos et al.) to allow exact sparsity with differentiability; switch to deterministic hard threshold p>0.5 at eval.

Metrics
- Training: peak memory, images/sec.
- Inference: latency per image for 50 steps, peak memory, FLOPs (fvcore), average active columns per step, CLIP score (image-text), FID on 30k COCO val images.
- Memory/FLOPs measured at batch=4 on single A100; also report batch=1 on 24 GB GPU.

Ablations (non-overlapping with Exp1)
- Gates: learned vs fixed schedule vs always-on.
- K in {2, 3}; G in {1, 2, 4} in latent space.
- Composer precision: fp16 vs bf16.

Acceptance criteria
- Avg active columns < 2.0 with K=3; FLOPs ↓ ≈45% vs full-depth.
- Latency speedup 1.4–1.7× vs baseline SD-UNet; CLIP within ±0.02 and FID within 5%.
- Peak inference memory < 50% of DeepCache at matched speed.

Implementation snippets

1) Latent model skeleton via diffusers

from diffusers import AutoencoderKL
vae = AutoencoderKL.from_pretrained("stabilityai/sd-vae-ft-mse", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16).cuda().eval()

# Encode RGB to latents, decode latents to RGB for eval
@torch.no_grad()
def encode_rgb(x):
    return vae.encode(x).latent_dist.sample() * 0.18215

@torch.no_grad()
def decode_latents(z):
    z = z / 0.18215
    return vae.decode(z).sample

2) Column gater (Hard-Concrete L0 optional)

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class ColumnGater(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_cols, cond_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(cond_dim+1, 128), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(128, num_cols))
    def forward(self, t_norm, text_emb):
        h = torch.cat([t_norm[:, None], text_emb], dim=1)
        logits = self.net(h)
        gates = torch.sigmoid(logits)
        return gates  # [B, K]

# Hard thresholding at eval
def hard_gate(gates, thresh=0.5):
    return (gates > thresh).float()

3) Integrating gates during forward

def forward_with_gates(model, xt, t, text_emb, stepsched):
    t_norm = t.float() / model.num_timesteps
    gates = model.gater(t_norm, text_emb)  # [B, K]
    out = 0
    for k, col in enumerate(model.columns):
        gk = gates[:, k].view(-1, 1, 1, 1)
        if model.training:
            out = out + gk * col(xt, t, text_emb)
        else:
            gk_h = hard_gate(gk)
            if gk_h.sum() > 0:
                out = out + gk_h * col(xt, t, text_emb)
    return out

4) Profiling FLOPs and latency/memory

from fvcore.nn import FlopCountAnalysis
import time

def measure_inference(model, sampler, cond, steps=50):

    return {
        'latency_s': time.time() - start,

# Rough FLOPs on a representative input

5) CLIP and FID on COCO
- Use open-clip ViT-g/H model for CLIP score against captions.
- clean-fid for FID with COCO val stats (compute once from real images encoded+decoded with same VAE to avoid VAE mismatch bias).

Expected outcome
- K=3 with learned gates yields ~45% FLOP reduction and 1.4–1.7× lower latency than baseline SD-UNet, with lower peak memory than DeepCache (no cache tensors), CLIP/FID parity.


=================================================================
Experiment 3 — 1024×1024 training feasibility on a single 24 GB GPU
=================================================================
Goal
- Demonstrate that RevMoDiff makes 1024² training feasible on a single 24 GB GPU, whereas ADM OOMs or requires crippling settings.
- Optional: 512² personalization via LoRA on 8 GB GPU (DreamBooth-style) to show low-memory finetuning.

Dataset
- ImageNet-1K resized to 1024². For feasibility, unconditional configuration; optionally class-conditional.

Baselines and settings
- Baseline ADM-UNet + checkpointing; attempt batch=1; log OOM or successful config.
- Ours: RevMoDiff with K=2, G=8, composer in fp16, EMA, grad accumulation to effective batch 8–16.

Protocol
- Hardware: single 24 GB GPU (RTX 3090/4090). torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32=True.
- Ours: use AMP fp16, gradient accumulation steps as needed, DDP disabled (single GPU). Use xformers memory-efficient attention if attention present.
- Measure forward+backward success, peak memory, step time, initial sample quality sanity after 50k steps.

Metrics
- Peak memory, images/sec (or iters/sec), stability (loss curve), sample grid for qualitative sanity.

Acceptance criteria
- RevMoDiff trains at 1024² with batch ≥ 1 within ≤ 24 GB peak; baseline ADM either OOMs or runs with severely reduced batch/throughput.

Implementation snippets

1) Feasibility harness

def can_train_1024(model):
    try:
        model = model.cuda()
        x0 = torch.randn(1, 3, 1024, 1024, device='cuda')
        t = torch.randint(0, model.num_timesteps, (1,), device='cuda')
        noise = torch.randn_like(x0)
        xt = model.q_sample(x0, t, noise)
        torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats()
        with torch.cuda.amp.autocast():
            out = model(xt, t, None)
            loss = F.mse_loss(out, noise)
        loss.backward()
        peak = torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()/1024**2
        print(f"OK @1024: peak {peak:.1f} MiB")
        return True
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print("Failed @1024:", e)
        return False

2) Training loop (single-GPU, grad accumulation)

scaler = GradScaler()
accum_steps = 8

for step, batch in enumerate(loader):
    x0, y = batch
    x0 = x0.cuda(non_blocking=True)
    t = torch.randint(0, model.num_timesteps, (x0.size(0),), device='cuda')
    noise = torch.randn_like(x0)
    xt = model.q_sample(x0, t, noise)
    with autocast():
        pred = model(xt, t, y if class_cond else None)
        loss = F.mse_loss(pred, noise) / accum_steps
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    if (step+1) % accum_steps == 0:
        scaler.step(optimizer)
        scaler.update()
        optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

3) Optional 512² personalization (LoRA on 8 GB)

                      target_modules=["composer.cond_to_AB.0", "composer.cond_to_AB.2", "final_conv"])

# Freeze base except LoRA adapters and output heads

    if 'lora_' not in n and 'final_conv' not in n:
        p.requires_grad_(False)

# DreamBooth: overfit few subject images with class prior preservation; batch=1; grad accum; AMP fp16

Expected outcome
- RevMoDiff fits 1024² training on ≤24 GB with K=2, G=8, whereas ADM is impractical. Optional LoRA finetuning fits ≤6–8 GB memory with competitive personalization quality to Hollowed Net.


=======================================
Global checks, fairness, and integration
=======================================
- Distributed training: Use accelerate for easy DDP + AMP; ensure gradient synchronization disabled for frozen teacher.
- torch.compile: Test compile("max-autotune") for additional speed; fall back if instability observed in reversible recomputation.
- xformers: Enable memory-efficient attention in attention-based coupling sub-blocks if used.
- Logging: wandb or TensorBoard to track memory, throughput, FID/IS/CLIP, EMA metrics, gate activations, average columns, FLOPs.
- Teacher choice: Use strong ADM for ImageNet experiments; for COCO latent, use SD-UNet as teacher to minimize train-test distribution shift.
- Sampler: Keep the same sampler (DDIM/DPMSolver++) and NFE when comparing models; report both 50 and 100 steps if feasible.
- Statistical confidence: For key metrics (FID/CLIP), run 3 seeds and report mean ± 95% CI; use 50k samples for FID at 256².

Sanity and failure-mode diagnostics
- Reversibility drift: If round-trip error exceeds 1e-4, reduce s scaling (tanh), insert actnorm, or use additive coupling in early layers.
- Composer instability: If loss spikes, reduce composer learning rate 10×, clip composer gradients, or restrict LoRA rank.
- Gate collapse: If gates collapse to shallow columns, lower α or warm-start with fixed schedule longer; add knowledge distillation at deeper layers.
- Throughput drops: Reduce G if too high; group-slicing increases sequential compute. Tune G to meet memory target with acceptable speed.

How the three experiments complement without redundancy
- Exp1 isolates architectural memory/parameter savings (gates off) and quality on ImageNet. It also runs orthogonal ablations (K/G/distillation/sharing) at 256² to quantify each design choice.
- Exp2 focuses on adaptive compute in latent space, linking gates to inference latency/memory without caches; uses a different task and evaluation (text-conditional CLIP/FID) and introduces L0 gating.
- Exp3 stresses feasibility at extreme resolution and low-resource personalization; it reuses the same backbone with memory-favoring settings (high G, K=2) and does not repeat quality parity tests.

Expected consolidated findings
- Peak training memory ↓ ~60% at 512² vs ADM+checkpoint; parameter count ↓ ~4×.
- ImageNet-256/512 quality parity (FID/IS/CLIP) with negligible degradation; throughput within ±10% for full-depth runs.
- Adaptive columns reduce FLOPs ~45% and speed up inference 1.6× on average, with <50% of DeepCache’s peak memory at similar speed because no cached features are stored.
- 1024² training feasible on a single 24 GB GPU; 512² personalization feasible on 8 GB via LoRA with quality on par with Hollowed Net.

This end-to-end plan implements RevMoDiff using widely available PyTorch libraries, details instrumentation for reliable measurement, and supplies modular code you can extend into full training scripts.
